description: Holy shit, if you haven't wrapped your ears around this cosmic country-pop mindfuck, you're missing one of the most beautifully twisted vocal marriages ever committed to wax - Nancy Sinatra's dead-eyed cool grinding against Lee Hazlewood's whiskey-soaked baritone like velvet sandpaper on a fever dream. This isn't some cutesy duet bullshit; it's full-on psychosexual Americana that makes Johnny Cash and June Carter sound like they're singing nursery rhymes at a church social. Hazlewood's arrangements are so perfectly demented and Nancy's delivery so icily seductive that you'll forget this thing came out on a major label and not some peyote-fueled desert commune's vanity imprint.

title: Tenor Saw Lives On: A Tribute To Tenor Saw
label: Sky High
description: This posthumous tribute to the late dancehall prophet finds various DJ disciples attempting to channel Tenor Saw's razor-sharp vocal attack and street-wise patois delivery, though most come off like karaoke versions of the real thing. The interview segments scattered throughout reveal more about the man's enduring influence on Jamaica's sound system culture than the musical recreations do, offering glimpses into how his "Ring The Alarm" single became the template for a generation of chatters who couldn't match his effortless flow over those killin' digital riddims. Sky High's heart is in the right place with this memorial, but nothing here captures the lightning-in-a-bottle urgency that made Tenor Saw's brief recording career so essential to the dancehall explosion of the mid-'80s.

title: Out There
label: Prestige, New Jazz, Prestige
description: Dolphy's reed-work here is like watching someone perform surgery with a chainsaw while reciting Verlaine – technically impossible yet somehow transcendent, with Ron Carter and Roy Haynes providing the kind of rhythmic cushion that makes even the most angular melodic excursions feel like coming home drunk at 4 AM. The man's alto and bass clarinet explorations on tracks like "Out There" sound like what would happen if Charlie Parker had been raised by Tibetan monks instead of Kansas City hustlers, all bent intervals and impossible grace notes that shouldn't work but absolutely fucking do. Essential document of a cat who was already living in 1975 while the rest of the world was still trying to figure out what happened to 1955.
